fields.meta_title: What Is the Trinity? One God in Three Persons
fields.description: The Trinity is the Christian understanding of God: one God, eternally Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Here is what it means, why it matters, and how it shapes the gospel.
fields.body_html:
The Trinity is the Christian understanding of who God is: one God, eternally existing as three persons — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It is not a riddle invented by theologians but the church’s faithful summary of how God has revealed himself in Scripture. There is one God, not three; and yet the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, each fully and truly, each distinct from the others, and all sharing one undivided divine nature. This is the deepest mystery of the faith, and also its greatest glory, for it means that God is, in his very being, a fellowship of love.

The word “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible, but the truth is woven through it from beginning to end. The doctrine simply holds together everything Scripture says about God without letting go of any of it. Let us trace how.

There is only one God

The starting point is unshakeable: the God of the Bible is one. Israel’s great confession rings through both Testaments: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Christianity is not a polytheism with three gods; it is fiercely monotheistic. Paul, a Jew steeped in that confession, insisted that “there is no God but one” (1 Corinthians 8:4). Whatever we say about Father, Son, and Spirit, we may never say it in a way that gives us more than one God.

This is the first guardrail. The Trinity is not the idea that three gods cooperate, nor that one God wears three masks at different times. It is the confession that the one true God exists eternally as three distinct persons who are each that one God. Hold that firmly, and the rest falls into place.

The Father, the Son, and the Spirit are each God

Yet this one God has revealed himself as three. The Father is unhesitatingly called God throughout Scripture — “one God, the Father, from whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6). No one disputes that. The wonder of the New Testament is that the same full deity is ascribed to the Son and to the Spirit.

Of the Son, John writes: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14). The Word was with God (distinct from the Father) and was God (fully divine). Jesus received worship, forgave sins, and claimed, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); when Thomas fell before the risen Christ crying “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), Jesus accepted it. And the Spirit, too, is divine and personal: to lie to the Holy Spirit, Peter said, is to “lie to God” (Acts 5:3–4). The Spirit is not an impersonal force but a person who teaches, grieves, and wills.

The three are distinct persons

The Father, Son, and Spirit are not three names for one person playing different roles. They are genuinely distinct, relating to one another in love. We see all three together, distinct yet inseparable, at the baptism of Jesus: the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice speaks from heaven, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16–17). Three persons, one scene, one God.

The distinctions run all through Jesus’ teaching. The Son prays to the Father; the Father sends the Son; and both send the Spirit. “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, and the Spirit is not the Father — and yet there are not three Gods, but one. This is the heart of the mystery, and the church has been content to confess it without pretending to exhaust it.

The Trinity is stamped on our salvation

Far from being an abstract puzzle, the Trinity is the very shape of the gospel. Our salvation is the work of all three persons together: the Father plans and sends, the Son accomplishes redemption, and the Spirit applies it to our hearts. Paul’s benediction gathers them into one blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14).

Consider what this means for the believer’s assurance. Your salvation does not rest on the effort of a single moment or the strength of your own grip, but on the united work of the whole Godhead bent toward your rescue. The Father chose you before the world began; the Son bought you with his blood; the Spirit sealed you and lives within you as the guarantee of what is to come. Three persons, one saving purpose, all set on bringing you safely home. A salvation held by the Trinity is a salvation that cannot fail.

This is why Jesus commanded his church to baptize “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) — note the singular “name,” one name held by three persons. To become a Christian is to be brought into the life of the triune God: adopted by the Father, united to the Son, and indwelt by the Spirit. Every prayer we pray runs along Trinitarian lines — we come to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. The doctrine is not a distraction from the gospel; it is the gospel’s architecture.

Three persons, working as one

The three persons of the Trinity never act against one another or apart from one another; they always work together, in perfect harmony. The Son does nothing independently of the Father — “the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19) — and the Spirit, in turn, glorifies the Son: “He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14). There is no rivalry in God, no competition for glory, only an eternal delight of each person in the others.

This mutual self-giving is the pattern of divine life. The Father loves and sends; the Son gladly obeys and gives himself; the Spirit points away from himself to the Son. Each honours the others. And this tells us something about the love at the centre of reality: it is not grasping but giving, not self-seeking but self-offering. When we are drawn into the life of God, we are drawn into that same current of humble, mutual love — which is why pride is so foreign to the Christian, and why servanthood is so like our God.

Why it matters that God is triune

The Trinity tells us something breathtaking about God’s very nature: that God is love, not merely that he loves. Before anything was created, before there was a universe to love, the Father loved the Son and the Son loved the Father in the fellowship of the Spirit. Jesus spoke of the Father loving him “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). Love is not something God learned or acquired; it is who he eternally is, because he has never been alone. A solitary god could not be love in himself; the triune God is.

This means the God who invites us to know him is not a distant, self-absorbed monarch but an overflowing fellowship of love that has opened itself to include us. And it means that when we have seen Jesus, we have truly seen God — for Jesus said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The face of God is the face of Christ, full of grace and truth.

Holding the mystery with humility

No illustration fully captures the Trinity, and every analogy eventually limps. That should not trouble us. If God could be entirely comprehended by creatures, he would not be much of a God. The early church laboured hard, especially against those who denied the full deity of the Son, to state the truth carefully — that the Son is not a lesser or created being but is himself God, of one substance with the Father. Their patient defence of this truth preserved the gospel itself, for only God can save, and only if Christ is truly God does his death truly redeem.

So we bow before a God greater than our minds can hold, and we worship. The Trinity is not a problem to be solved but a glory to be adored — one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the fountain of all love, who has made room in his own eternal fellowship for us. “There is one body and one Spirit... one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4–6). We will spend eternity discovering the depths of this God and never reach the bottom of his goodness. To him be glory forever.
